title: More useful after death
hookLine: dying, Dominic promised his brothers he'd help them more from heaven

cards: Bologna, a friary, a hot summer. The founder is dying. Dominic, who by tradition walked the roads barefoot, and once talked all night with an innkeeper, lies on the floor, by tradition on sackcloth, too weak to rise.
Around him his brothers are crying. They are young, the order is young, and they don't know how they'll manage without him. What do you say to people who are about to lose you?
Dominic's answer was about the future, and it sounds almost cheeky.

teach.h: DON'T WEEP. I'LL BE MORE USEFUL THEN.
teach.b: An early life of Dominic, written by Jordan of Saxony, who led the order after him, tells it this way. Dominic saw his brothers weeping and told them not to.
He would be more useful to them after his death, he said, than he had been in life. Not: I'll always be in your hearts. Not: carry on my work.
But: I'm not leaving the job. I'm changing posts. Back on day ninety-six you met the cloud of witnesses; this is where it leads.
The promise rests on a Catholic belief called the communion of saints.
Catholics hold that the Church is one family across death: the living on earth, the dead being made ready, and the saints with God. And family members pray for one another.
So asking a saint for help is, for Catholics, like asking a friend to pray for you, only the friend is now close to God.
Hebrews, in the Douay-Rheims, pictures believers running their race "having so great a cloud of witnesses over our head."
Christians don't all read this the same way. Catholic and Orthodox tradition asks the saints to pray.
Some Protestant churches teach that prayer should go to God alone, and they honor the saints as examples rather than asking their help. Dominicans took Dominic at his word.

teach.h: O SPEM MIRAM: O WONDERFUL HOPE.
teach.b: Their tradition sings a short Latin antiphon to him that begins O spem miram, O wonderful hope, recalling this promise.

teach.h: SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.
teach.b: A goodbye that turned into a job description.

how: Catholics ask the saints to pray for them, in private prayer and in the Church's litanies; Dominicans traditionally sing the antiphon O Spem Miram to Saint Dominic.

games.q: you're Dominic, dying on the floor of the friary. your young brothers are weeping. what do you tell them?
o: remember me, and carry on as best you can.
don't weep: I'll be more useful to you after death.
nothing; you're too weak to speak.
games.why: Jordan of Saxony records that he told them not to weep, because he would help them more after his death than in life.

practice: If you pray to the saints, choose one, Dominic or a saint you love, and ask them plainly to pray for one thing you're carrying today.
If that isn't your practice, bring to mind someone who has died who helped you, and notice where their help is still at work in you: a phrase you still use.
If a loss is heavy right now, you don't have to carry it alone; in the US, 988 answers day and night, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: More useful after death. Dominic's last promise to his weeping brothers: he wasn't leaving them, he was changing posts. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: O wonderful hope. The opening of the Dominicans' antiphon to Saint Dominic, recalling his last promise.

carryVoice: Your line: more useful then. In his promise, the young brothers weren't left on their own. I'll be here tomorrow.
